summary: Lens-diverse task review of one diff, each finding adversarially verified by a skeptic panel

prior_findings.note: The orchestrator now has an explicit `redis: condition: service_healthy` dependency in docker-compose.yml. The strict profile is covered because the render test runs under dev and strict. Every other app service with uses_redis=True (safety, therapy, diagnosis, memory) is covered, and so is user-service. personality, notification and analytics have no Redis code at all. The scan is derived by AST from the IF-01 ServiceRuntimeSpec calls. A new guard test pins the five IF-01 services with a superset check, so the scan cannot silently find nothing. tests/deploy: 70 passed, 10 skipped.

Partly closed. run() now has one stop path, _stop_run. It removes the one-off container, bounds the waits, kills and waits on the process, and covers KeyboardInterrupt. Closing the pipes can still hang forever when a grandchild holds them (see WS033F2-CLO-1), so the second-timeout case is not fully bounded.

findings.problem: _stop_run closes proc.stdout and proc.stderr in `finally` with no bound. On Windows, communicate() reads those pipes in background threads. If a grandchild process still holds the write ends, the reader thread stays blocked inside read() and holds the BufferedReader lock. `pipe.close()` then blocks on that lock and never returns. That is the exact case the code comment describes: the compose plugin keeps the pipes open after the docker CLI is killed.
findings.failure_scenario: I reproduced it on this machine with the venv Python. A parent process spawned a grandchild that held the inherited pipes. I called communicate(timeout=1) twice, then kill(), then wait(), then close() on both pipes in a thread. The close thread was still alive after 8 s. In run(), a second timeout where the plugin has not exited blocks in pipe.close() forever, so the call neither raises ComposeProjectError nor returns. The unit test does not catch this because it uses fake pipes whose close() returns immediately. The same hang applies on the KeyboardInterrupt path.
findings.fix: Close the pipes from a daemon thread and join it with a short timeout. Alternatively, skip closing when the communicate reader threads are still alive. Alternatively, create the Popen with pipes that are not shared (for example, redirect output to temp files) so no reader thread can block close(). Add a test with a real grandchild that holds the pipes.
findings.evidence: D:\tmp\pipetest.py repro (deleted after the run) printed `hung`. conftest.py _stop_run, the `finally` block, closes both pipes inline. The mock `_Pipe.close` in tests/deploy/test_mvp_118_redis_auth.py returns instantly.

votes.reason: I reproduced the hang. With the venv Python on Windows, I spawned a parent that starts a grandchild holding the inherited pipes. I called communicate(timeout=1) twice, then kill() and wait(). Closing proc.stdout from a thread was still blocked after 5 s, and the script printed "hung". The close blocks because the communicate reader thread holds the BufferedReader lock. `_stop_run` in tests/deploy/conftest.py (finally block, around line 185) closes both pipes inline with no bound. The code comment says the compose plugin keeps the pipes open after the CLI is killed, which is the scenario I reproduced. A second timeout where the plugin has not exited therefore hangs the test run instead of raising ComposeProjectError, which is the problem the CLO-2 fix was meant to prevent. The fake pipes in the unit test return from close() immediately, so they would not catch it. I did not run the tests/deploy suite, and I did not check how `run()` calls `_stop_run`.

I reproduced the hang. In a venv Python on Windows, a parent spawned a grandchild that held the inherited stdout and stderr pipes. I called communicate(timeout=1) twice, then kill() and wait(). A thread then called close() on both pipes, and it was still alive after 6 s, so the script printed "hung". The `finally` block in `_stop_run` (tests/deploy/conftest.py, around line 185) does the same inline close, so the second-timeout path in `run()` can block forever. That is the case the docstring describes, where the compose plugin keeps the pipes open after the CLI is killed. I found no ruling or later plan task that makes this intended or out of scope. The hang only occurs with real infrastructure, which is a minor limit on severity. Important is still reasonable, because it defeats the fix for the earlier finding WS033F1-CLO-2.

I reproduced the hang. In _stop_run (conftest.py, around lines 165-188), proc.stdout and proc.stderr are closed inline in `finally`. I ran communicate() twice with a 1 s timeout, then kill() and wait(), then closed both pipes in a thread while a grandchild still held the pipes. After 6 s the close thread was still alive. Reader threads from communicate() hold the BufferedReader lock, so close() blocks until the grandchild exits. This is the case the code comment describes, where the compose plugin outlives the killed docker CLI. The effect is that run() hangs instead of raising ComposeProjectError. It only happens when the plugin has not exited by the second timeout, and it hits only the opt-in real-infra tests. I did not run tests/deploy. The "important" severity is reasonable.
